# Car Radio Stopped Working: Diagnosing an Electrical Short in a 2001 Mazda ProtegÃ©

When a user plugs a USB charger into a vehicle's accessory port and the entire audio system cuts out immediately, the issue is rarely a software glitch or a simple fuse blow. In your specific case with the 2001 Mazda ProtegÃ©, the symptomsâthe radio shutting off simultaneously with the loss of power to the USB outletâpoint directly to an electrical short circuit at the point of connection.

The accessory port in vehicles like the ProtegÃ© is typically powered by the ignition switch but shares a common ground and often a single fused power line for both the data/charging circuitry (if integrated) and the main 12V output. When you inserted the USB charger, the metal contacts inside the socket likely touched the internal housing or another pin due to debris, a bent tab, or a manufacturing defect in the port itself. This created a low-resistance path between the live 12V line and the chassis ground.

Modern chargers often include protection circuits, but older vehicles or poorly manufactured USB adapters might not trigger an immediate shutdown before the surge propagates upstream. The fuse protecting that circuit blew instantly to prevent damage to the wiring harness or the alternator. In many Mazda models from this era, the accessory power is fused in the main junction box under the dash or in the engine bay fuse block. You need to locate the specific fuse labeled "ACC," "Radio," or sometimes just a generic 15A or 20A inline fuse near the port.

If that fuse was indeed blown, it explains why neither the radio nor the USB outlet has power. The key distinction here is that the radio didn't just go to standby; it shut off completely. This indicates a catastrophic failure of voltage regulation rather than a user setting issue. Replacing the fuse with one of the same amperage rating will restore basic function, but only if the short within the port itself has been resolved.

The most critical step before re-fusing is inspecting the accessory socket. Remove the trim panel covering the USB port (usually held by clips or screws) and examine the internal pins. If the metal housing of the USB adapter was pushed into the connector, it may have bridged the power and ground terminals. In some cases, the plastic insulator inside the socket has cracked, allowing the contacts to touch. You must clean out any debris and ensure no metal from the charger is stuck between the pins.

If the port's internal wiring is severed or the housing is melted from the heat of the short, simply replacing the fuse will result in an immediate burnout again. In this scenario, you would need to splice in a new inline fuse holder closer to the battery or the main junction block if the factory fuse location is inaccessible or unreliable. Alternatively, swapping out the entire accessory socket assembly might be necessary if the internal contacts are damaged beyond repair.

It is also worth noting that some aftermarket USB adapters are not isolated from the 12V line properly. If your adapter has a built-in battery or complex logic board that draws excessive current upon startup, it could have pulled down the voltage on the shared rail, triggering the radio's internal protection and blowing the fuse. Ensure any new charger you use is high-quality, preferably with an LED indicator that confirms stable power delivery before fully engaging with the car's electrical system.

By methodically checking the fuse block, inspecting the physical integrity of the accessory port, and ensuring the short is physically removed, you can restore functionality without needing a complex diagnostic tool or professional repair shop intervention.
